# [LumiLettuce] Descriptive & Inferential Statistics

## I. Load libraries and inspect data set

Load the necessary libraries and create path to tidy data set. Read the tidy data set file in the form of RDS. This is better than .csv version because the RDS can save particular objects. For example, it preserves the variable type of each column making analysis easier.

```{r 00_load}

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)      # to make figures
library(kableExtra)   # to make tables
library(factoextra)
library(patchwork)
library(phyloseq)
library(gt)
library(ggsci)
library(RColorBrewer) # to make figures

# Use the function 'here' to create a path to tidy data set
data_tidy_path <- here::here("data/processed") 
    #data_tidy_path
    #list.files(data_tidy_path) 

# the RDS file is generated by companion script to tidy data (blueC_data_tidying_R)
lumilettuce <- readRDS(file.path(data_tidy_path,"full_data.rds")) 
    
glimpse(lumilettuce) 
head(lumilettuce)

```

There are 24 columns and 18,988 rows in this data set. It includes both the microbiome data and the metadata. There are categorical and continuous variables.

## II. Abiotic environment

### 1. Abiotic summary table

Many of the metadata variables are continuous environmental parameters. They help us to understand the context. Some, could also be interesting to explore later on to see if there are correlations in the data associated with these continuous variables. This table compares the metrics (mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, minimum, and maximum) for the continuous environmental variables of the data set across all diel phases between the two sites. This helps us establish the baseline environmental conditions across sites and time of day.

```{r 01_summary_table}

table_summary_continuous <- lumilettuce                                     |>
  filter(!is.na(sample_id), !is.na(diel_phase), !is.na(site_name), !is.na(temp_degC), !is.na(salinity_psu), !is.na(dissolved_oxygen_mg_L), !is.na(pH), !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s))                                                    |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                     |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols        = c(temp_degC, dissolved_oxygen_mg_L, pH, salinity_psu,      
           PAR_umol_photons_m2_s),
           names_to = "Variable",
           values_to = "Value")                                             |>
  # Change the name of the Variable column to make it better suited for a table
  mutate(
    Variable    = case_when(
      Variable  == "temp_degC" ~ "Temperature (°C)",
      Variable  == "dissolved_oxygen_mg_L" ~ "Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)",
      Variable  == "pH" ~ "pH",
      Variable  == "salinity_psu" ~ "Salinity (PSU)",
      Variable  == "PAR_umol_photons_m2_s" ~ "PAR (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹)",
      TRUE ~ Variable)
    )                                                                       |>
  # There will be a top-header and a sub-header for site name and descriptive   
  # statistic variable, respectively
  group_by(diel_phase, Variable, site_name)                                             |>
  summarise(
    Mean        = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    SD          = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median      = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), 
    IQR         = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Min - Max` = sprintf("%.2f - %.2f", min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), max(Value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups     = "drop")                                                   |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = site_name,
    values_from = c(Mean, SD, Median, IQR, `Min - Max`),
    names_glue  = "{site_name}_{.value}")                                   |>
 arrange(diel_phase, Variable)                                              |>
  select(
    diel_phase, Variable,
    Pescalgarve_Mean, Pescalgarve_SD, Pescalgarve_Median, Pescalgarve_IQR, `Pescalgarve_Min - Max`,
    `Ria de Alvor_Mean`, `Ria de Alvor_SD`, `Ria de Alvor_Median`, `Ria de Alvor_IQR`, `Ria de Alvor_Min - Max`
  )

# This is not the final table
View(table_summary_continuous)

table_summary_continuous                                                    |>
  select(-diel_phase)                                                       |>
  kbl(
    # Sub-headers for metrics
    col.names   = c("Variable", 
                    "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR", "Min - Max", 
                    "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR", "Min - Max"),
    align       = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_classic(
    full_width  = FALSE, 
    html_font   = "Times New Roman",
    font_size   = 13)                                                       |>
  # Top header spanning across site groups
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Pescalgarve" = 5, "Ria de Alvor" = 5))       |>
  pack_rows("Dawn", 1, 5)                                                   |>
  pack_rows("Noon", 6, 10)                                                  |>
  pack_rows("Dusk", 11, 15)                                                 |>
  pack_rows("Midnight", 16, 20)                                             |>
  
  # Save this table as a .png in correct folder in directory to add to manuscript
  save_kable(file = "../output/tables/table_summary_continuous.png", zoom = 3)

```

When comparing between the two sites, we can already see that that the standard variation is 0 at all times for Ria de Alvor, which makes sense because there is a sample size n=1 for all site/diel phase combination. Dissolved oxygen (DO) and pH are quite similar in both sites. The largest differences for sites are pH, salinity, and PAR.

DO, salinity, and pH remain stable across all time points. PAR varies a lot because it remains low at dawn, dusk, and midnight, with the lowest values at dawn, but then has a peak increase at noon. This pattern is consistent across both sites. Temperature appears to fluctuate slightly during the day.

### 2. Boxplots for continuous environmental variables

The continuous environmental variables temperature, PAR, and salinity showed interesting variation in the table. These boxplots explore their variation across site and diel phase.

```{r 02_boxplot_temp}

# Remove NAs
boxplot_env_data <- lumilettuce                                            |>
  distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE)                                    |>
  filter(!is.na(diel_phase), !is.na(site_name), !is.na(temp_degC), !is.na(salinity_psu), !is.na(PAR_umol_photons_m2_s)) |>
  # To remove the water samples
  filter(sample_type != "Water filter" | is.na(sample_type)) 

# Boxplot for temperature
boxplot_temp <- ggplot(boxplot_env_data, aes(x = diel_phase,y = temp_degC, fill = site_name, colour = site_name)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha           = 0.2, # opacity
    outlier.shape   = NA, # no need to show outliers
    width           = 0.5,
    position        = position_dodge(width=0.75)
  ) +
  # Add a diamond shape for the mean of each box
  stat_summary(
    aes(group       = site_name),           
    fun             = mean,
    geom            = "point",
    shape           = 23,                       
    size            = 3.5,
    colour          = "black",                 
    fill            = "black",                  
    position        = position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position        = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width =0.15, dodge.width=0.75),
    size            = 2.5,
    alpha           = 0.3,
  ) +
  # Teal for Pescalgarve and orchid for Ria de Alvor
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Pescalgarve"="#008080", "Ria de Alvor"="#DA70D6")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("Pescalgarve"="#008080", "Ria de Alvor"="#DA70D6")) +
  theme_classic(base_size =12) +
  labs(
    x               = "Diel Phase",
    y               = "Temperature (ºC)",
    fill            = "Site Name",
    colour          = "Site Name"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title      = element_text(face="bold"),
    axis.text       = element_text(colour="black"),
    legend.position = "right",
    lengend.title   = element_text(face="bold")
  )

# Display temperature boxplot
boxplot_temp

# Save the temperature boxplot
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/boxplot_temp.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)

```

There are 9 observations for each box with 3 unique values for each box of Pescalgarve. A black diamond symbolizing the mean was added to each box. Ria de Alvor only has 9 of the same measurements (repeated) for each diel phase.

At Pescalgarve, the mean water temperature is at around 13ºC at midnight and then decreases at dawn before increasing steadily through noon reaching its peak at dusk. The Ria de Alvor has a different pattern. The mean water temperatures are higher than Pescalgarve with peaks greater tenmperatures at midnight and noon and lower temperatures at dawn and dusk.

## III. Categorical variables

### 1. Barplot of order relative abundance

The *Ulva*-associated microbiota has been characterized via Nanopore sequencing and subsequent software programs. The following barplot demonstrates the relative abundance of each order within each seaweed sample collected. This barplot shows the 15 most dominant orders of bacteria in all seaweed samples, the rest is denoted as "Others".

```{r 05_barplot_order}

order_data <- lumilettuce                                                                               |>
  # Filter out positive control "CM" and water samples ending in "w"
  filter((sample_id != "CM" & !str_ends(sample_id, regex("w", ignore_case = TRUE))) | is.na(sample_id)) |>
  group_by(sample_id)                                                                                   |>
  mutate(sample_total          = sum(count))                                                            |>
  ungroup()                                                                                             |>
  # Calculate percentage
  mutate(rel_abund             = (count / sample_total) * 100)                                          |>
  # Keep top 15 orders and group the rest into "Other"
  mutate(order_top             = fct_lump_n(order, n = 15, w = rel_abund, other_level = "Other"))       |>
  # Group and summarize relative abundance per order_top
  group_by(sample_id, order_top)                                                                        |>
  summarise(rel_abund          = sum(rel_abund), .groups = "drop")                                      |>
  # Format order_top factor levels (controls the legend order)
  mutate(
    order_top                  = fct_reorder(order_top, rel_abund, .fun = sum, .desc = TRUE),
    order_top                  = fct_relevel(order_top, "Other", after = Inf)
  )                                                                                                     |>
  # Place relative abundances in a decreasing order from bottom to top with "Other" completely at the bottom
  arrange(sample_id, order_top == "Other", rel_abund)                                                   |>
  mutate(stack_group           = fct_inorder(paste(sample_id, order_top, sep = "___"))
         )

# Create the plot using ggplot2
barplot_order <- ggplot(order_data, aes(x = sample_id, y = rel_abund, fill = order_top, group = stack_group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.9) +
  # This colour palette has high contrast and at least 15 colours
  scale_fill_d3("category20") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x                          = "Sample ID",
    y                          = "Relative Abundance (%)",
    fill                       = "Order"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x                = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 6),
    legend.position            = "bottom"
  )
# View the barplot
barplot_order

# Save the order barplot
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/barplot_order.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

The samples on the left side are the ones collected in Pescalgarve as denoted by the fist letter "P", and the samples on the right side are from Ria de Alvor as denoted by the first letter "R". The microbial community in Pescalgarve appears to be dominated by the *Cytophagales* and the *Flavobacteriales* orders. The *Pseudomonadales* order is also heavily present, although at a lesser degree than the other two previously mentionned. The microbial community in Ria de Alvor is widely dominated by *Pseudomonadales*. The orders *Enterobacterales* and *Cytophagales* are also dominant in some samples of Ria de Alvor. The order Chitinophagales is one of the major players in Pescalgarve but has a much smaller relative abundance in Ria de Alvor.

### 2. Order stacked barplots by site and diel phase

This barplot is looking at the relative abundance (%) of orders for each dile phase in both environments. It shows only the 10 dominant orders and the rest is categorized as "Other".

```{r 06_barplot_order_diel}

order_data_diel <- lumilettuce                                                                          |>
  # Remove the water samples, the community standard, and all NAs
  filter(!is.na(site_name), !is.na(diel_phase))                                                         |>
  filter((sample_id != "CM" & !str_ends(sample_id, regex("w", ignore_case = TRUE))) | is.na(sample_id)) |>
  filter(sample_type != "Water filter" | is.na(sample_type))                                            |>
  # Rename the NAs to Unassigned
  mutate(order                    = replace_na(as.character(order), "Unassigned"))                      |>
  # Calculate sample totals and relative abundance
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, order)                                                     |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count), .groups = "drop")                                                 |>
  group_by(sample_id)                                                                                   |>
  mutate(rel_abund                = (total_count / sum(total_count)) * 100)                             |>
  ungroup()                                                                                             |>
  # Select 10 dominant orders and the rest is grouped under "Other" 
  mutate(order_top                = fct_lump_n(order, n = 10, w = rel_abund, other_level = "Other"))    |>
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, order_top)                                                 |>
  summarise(rel_abund = sum(rel_abund), .groups = "drop")                                               |>
  # Complete missing combinations per sample
  complete(sample_id, order_top, fill = list(rel_abund = 0))                                            |>
  group_by(sample_id)                                                                                   |>
  fill(site_name, diel_phase, .direction = "downup")                                                    |>
  ungroup()                                                                                             |>
  # Calculate mean relative abundance per site and diel phase
  group_by(site_name, diel_phase, order_top)                                                            |>
  summarise(mean_rel_abund        = mean(rel_abund, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")                    |>
  # Ensure each group adds up to 100%
  group_by(site_name, diel_phase)                                                                       |>
  mutate(mean_rel_abund           = (mean_rel_abund / sum(mean_rel_abund)) * 100)                       |>
  ungroup()                                                                                             |>
  # Ordering
  mutate(
    diel_phase                    = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Midnight", "Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk")),
    order_top                     = fct_reorder(order_top, mean_rel_abund, .fun = sum, .desc = TRUE),
    order_top                     = fct_relevel(order_top, "Other", after = Inf)
  )

# Create the plot with ggplot2
ggplot(order_data_diel, aes(x = diel_phase, y = mean_rel_abund, fill = order_top))         +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2, width = 0.8)              +
  facet_wrap(~ site_name)                                                                  +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100.1), expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25))     +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette       = "Paired")                                              + 
  theme_minimal(base_size         = 12)                                                    +
  labs(
    y                             = "Mean Relative Abundance (%)", 
    x                             = "Diel Phase", 
    fill                          = "Order"
  )                                                                                        +
  theme(
    axis.title                    = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text                     = element_text(color = "black"),
    strip.text                    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position               = "right",
    legend.title                  = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# Save the order barplot
dir.create("../output/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "../output/figures/barplot_order_diel.png",
  width    = 8.5,
  height   = 5.5,
  dpi      = 300
)

```

From this, we can see that *Pseudomonadales* is the dominant order in Ria de Alvor at all diel phases. In Pescalgarve, *Flavobacteriales*, *Cytophagales*, and *Pseudomonadales* share the dominance at all diel phases. The mean relative abundance of each order appears to be relatively stable across all diel phases in both environments, with the exception of the order *Bacillales*. This order of bacteria is found in low levels at dawn, noon, and dusk, but they have a peak at midnight. Midnight is the time point of nocturnal respiration. This group is possibly recruited for their function in this metabolic process.

```{r 02_domtable}
# 1. Prepare the Top 1 Genus data
top_1_genus_data <- df |>
  filter(sample_type == "Ulva") |>
  # Average replicates to get mean relative abundance per Genus
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, genus) |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  mutate(rel_abund = (total_count / sum(total_count)) * 100) |>
  group_by(site_name, diel_phase, genus) |>
  summarise(mean_rel_abund = mean(rel_abund), .groups = "drop") |>
  # Select the winner (#1) for each Site and Time
  group_by(site_name, diel_phase) |>
  slice_max(mean_rel_abund, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

# 2. Build the Pretty GT Table
top_1_genus_table <- top_1_genus_data |>
  gt(groupname_col = "site_name") |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Dominant Community Members**"),
    subtitle = "The #1 Bacterial Genus by Mean Relative Abundance"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = mean_rel_abund,
    decimals = 1,
    pattern = "{x}%" 
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    diel_phase = "Time of Day",
    genus = "Dominant Genus",
    mean_rel_abund = "Avg. Abundance"
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    heading.background.color = "#005f73", # Burgundy
    column_labels.background.color = "#f8f9fa",
    table.font.size = px(16),
    row_group.font.weight = "bold"
  ) |>
  # Style headers to match your plot
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "#005f73"), 
    locations = cells_row_groups(groups = "Pescalgarve")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "orange"), 
    locations = cells_row_groups(groups = "Ria do Alvor")
  )

# 3. View the table
top_1_genus_table
```

```{r 02_boxplot}

# 1. Filter and prepare the data
richness_data <- microbiome3 |>  # Use your cleaned data frame
  filter(
    site_name != "Unknown", 
    diel_phase != "Unknown",
    genus != "Unknown",       # Also removes "Unknown" from the richness count
    sample_type == "Ulva"     # Focusing on the Ulva story
  ) |>
  # Set chronological order for the X-axis

                             levels = c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight"))) |>
  group_by(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase) |>
  summarise(richness = n_distinct(genus), .groups = "drop")

  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.shape = 21, outlier.fill = "white") +
  # Custom Ocean Colors: Deep Teal and Ocean Blue
```

```{r 05_pcoa_loc}
# 1. Clean and Prepare
df <- microbiome |> 
  filter(sample_type == "Ulva", site_name != "Unknown") |>
  # Crucial: Convert metadata to factors here so the plot legend is ordered correctly
  mutate(
    diel_phase = factor(diel_phase, levels = c("Dawn", "Noon", "Dusk", "Midnight")),
    site_name = as.factor(site_name)
  )

# A. OTU Table (Counts)
otu_mat <- df |>
  select(sample_id, genus, count) |>
  group_by(sample_id, genus) |> 
  summarise(count = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |> # Ensure no duplicate genus/sample rows
  pivot_wider(names_from = genus, values_from = count, values_fill = 0) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id") |>
  as.matrix()

# B. Tax Table (Classification)
tax_mat <- df |>
  select(superkingdom, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus) |>
  distinct(genus, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  column_to_rownames("genus") |>
  as.matrix()

# C. Sample Data (Metadata) - MUST be wrapped in sample_data()
# We ensure the row names match the otu_mat row names exactly
s_data <- df |>
  select(sample_id, site_name, morphotype, diel_phase) |>
  distinct() |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# D. Build the Phyloseq Object
# We explicitly convert components to phyloseq classes
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(otu_mat, taxa_are_rows = FALSE), 
  sample_data(s_data), 
  tax_table(tax_mat)
)

# --- VERIFICATION ---
# Run this to make sure 'site_name' is actually inside the object:
sample_variables(ps) 

# --- PLOTTING ---
# 2. Run Ordination
ps_pcoa <- ordinate(ps, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# 3. Plot (Notice the quotes around "site_name")
plot_ordination(ps, ps_pcoa, color = "site_name", shape = "diel_phase") +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = site_name), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#005f73", "Ria do Alvor" = "orange")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Pescalgarve" = "#005f73", "Ria do Alvor" = "orange")) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = 24, # Triangle Up
    "Noon"     = 21, # Circle
    "Dusk"     = 25, # Triangle Down
    "Midnight" = 8   # Star
  )) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    color = "Sampling Site",   # Renames the color legend
    shape = "Time of Day",     # Renames the shape legend
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold") # Makes legend titles stand out
  )

     
```

```{r 06_pcoa_pescalgarve}
# 1. Subset the phyloseq object to only include Pescalgarve
ps_pesc <- subset_samples(ps, site_name == "Pescalgarve")

# 2. Re-run the ordination
ps_pcoa_pesc <- ordinate(ps_pesc, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# 3. Plot with matching Ellipses and a MERGED legend
plot_ordination(ps_pesc, ps_pcoa_pesc, color = "diel_phase") +
  # Map color, shape, and fill to the same variable
  geom_point(aes(shape = diel_phase, fill = diel_phase), size = 6, alpha = 0.9) +
  
  # Ellipses (show.legend = FALSE keeps the shaded area out of the tiny legend icons)
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = diel_phase), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  # 1. Shape Scale (The Name "Time of Day" must match exactly in all three)
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = 24, # Triangle Up
    "Noon"     = 21, # Circle
    "Dusk"     = 25, # Triangle Down
    "Midnight" = 8   # Star
  )) +
  
  # 2. Color Scale
  scale_color_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = "#C8A2C8", # Lilac
    "Noon"     = "#BDB76B", # Khaki
    "Dusk"     = "#800020", # Burgundy
    "Midnight" = "#2E2E2E"  # Dark Grey
  )) +
  
  # 3. Fill Scale
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Time of Day", values = c(
    "Dawn"     = "#C8A2C8", 
    "Noon"     = "#BDB76B", 
    "Dusk"     = "#800020", 
    "Midnight" = "#2E2E2E"
  )) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Axis 1",
    y = "Axis 2"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right" # You can change this to "bottom" if you want more width
  )
```

```{r 08_pcoa_morphotype}

# 1. Prepare Metadata (Ensuring 'morphotype' is included this time)
s_data <- df |>
  select(sample_id, site_name, diel_phase, morphotype) |> 
  distinct() |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# 2. Rebuild the Phyloseq Object
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(otu_mat, taxa_are_rows = FALSE), 
  sample_data(s_data), 
  tax_table(tax_mat)
)

# 3. Run Ordination (Default is Axis 1 and 2)
ps_pcoa <- ordinate(ps, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# 4. Create the Plot
plot_ordination(ps, ps_pcoa, color = "morphotype", shape = "diel_phase") +
  # Ellipses in the background
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = morphotype), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  # Points with celestial shapes and colors
  geom_point(aes(fill = morphotype), size = 5, stroke = 1, alpha = 0.9) +  
  
  # Colors for Morphotypes
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Broad Blade" = "#800020", "Narrow Thalli" = "#BDB76B", "Filamentous" = "#C8A2C8")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Broad Blade" = "#800020", "Narrow Thalli" = "#BDB76B", "Filamentous" = "#C8A2C8")) +
  
  # Celestial Shape Mapping
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "Dawn"     = 24, # Triangle Up
    "Noon"     = 21, # Circle
    "Dusk"     = 25, # Triangle Down
    "Midnight" = 8   # Star
  )) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    color = "Morphotype",
    fill = "Morphotype",
    shape = "Time of Day"
  ) +
  # Ensures the legend icons match the points
  guides(fill = "none", color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21)))


```
